kunyah: Dhu al-Janahayn — the one with two wings
era: Spokesman before the Negus — Martyr of Mu'tah
teaser: He spent seven years abroad speaking for a Prophet he could not see, and less than a year at home before Mu'tah.
quran_mention: The ayah under which the migration to Abyssinia was made: «وَأَرْضُ اللَّهِ وَاسِعَةٌ» — 'and the earth of Allah is spacious' (39:10)

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: Abu Talib's son, Ali's full brother
layers.content:
His father was Abu Talib — whose given name, Ibn Sa'd records, was Abd Manaf ibn Abd al-Muttalib. That makes Ja'far a first cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, and a member of the household that took the orphaned Muhammad in and later stood between him and Quraysh for years.

His mother was Fatima bint Asad ibn Hashim, which means Ali ibn Abi Talib was not merely his brother but his full brother, same mother and same father. Ja'far was the elder of the two.

He married Asma bint Umays, of Khath'am — a woman whose own later life reads like a map of the early community, since after Ja'far's death she married Abu Bakr and bore him Muhammad, and after Abu Bakr's death she married Ali and bore him Yahya and Awn. When Abu Bakr was dying he left instructions that Asma should wash his body.

The corpus is thin on Ja'far's boyhood, and that gap is worth naming rather than filling. What the records do preserve is how the Prophet ﷺ spoke of him to strangers. In a letter carried to the king of Abyssinia there is a line in his own dictation: 'I have dispatched my cousin, Ja'far, with a group of Muslims to you, so be generous towards them and do not oppress them.'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (letter to the Negus, from al-Bayhaqi via Ibn Ishaq)

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: The earth of Allah is spacious
layers.content:
The persecution in Makkah began in earnest in the fourth year of the mission and got worse by the month. By the middle of the fifth year it had become unbearable, and Surah az-Zumar came with a line that the Muslims read as permission: the earth of Allah is spacious, and only the patient are given their reward without reckoning.

The Prophet ﷺ knew that the ruler of Abyssinia was a just man who would not wrong those under his authority, so he allowed his followers to leave. A first party of twelve men and four women went in Rajab. Later, when the torture intensified, a much larger group followed — eighty-three men and around nineteen women, moving fast enough that Quraysh could not stop them. Ja'far was among the emigrants to Abyssinia.

Understand what leaving cost. These were people whose entire identity was a place: the Haram, the House, the clan. Migration meant crossing a sea to a Christian kingdom whose language they did not speak, with no promise of return.

Quraysh did not let it go. They sent Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a — both still idolaters at the time — with expensive gifts for the king and his bishops, having already bought the sympathy of some of the court, to demand that the refugees be handed back.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 39:10 — 'Good is for those who do good in this world, and Allah's earth is spacious. Only those who are patient shall receive their rewards in full, without reckoning'
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham and Zad al-Ma'ad

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: He stood in a foreign court and spoke for a man who was not there
layers.content:
The Negus summoned the Muslims and asked them directly: what is this religion that has made you leave your people, without entering mine or any other. Ja'far stood up.

He did not begin with proofs. He began with a confession. 'O king, we were an ignorant people. We worshipped idols and ate the meat of dead carcasses. We were accustomed to lewd behaviour, to severing the ties of kinship, neglecting our neighbours, and the strong among us consumed the property of the weak.' Then Allah sent a Messenger whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness and chastity they already knew. He listed what they had been commanded: truthful speech, returning what is entrusted, keeping kinship ties, kindness to a neighbour, no unlawful bloodshed, no consuming an orphan's wealth, no slandering chaste women, prayer, charity, fasting.

Asked whether he had any of the revelation with him, he recited the opening of Surah Maryam. The king and his bishops wept until the tears ran into the Negus' beard, and he said it seemed these words and what was revealed to Jesus came from the same source. He refused to hand them over.

The envoys came back the next day claiming the Muslims blasphemed Jesus. Ja'far stood again: he is the servant of Allah, His Messenger, His spirit and His word cast into Maryam. The gifts were returned and the delegation sent home.
layers.quran_ref: Surah Maryam (19) — Ja'far recited its opening verses, the account of Yahya and Isa
layers.source: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, summarised from Ibn Hisham 1/334-338

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Mu'tah — three thousand against a reported two hundred thousand
layers.content:
Ibn Sa'd is precise about how long Ja'far was away: he emigrated before the brotherhood pairs were even made in Madinah, and 'he came seven years later.' The Negus sent him home at the Prophet's request and he reached him at Khaybar. He had roughly a year.

For the Mu'tah expedition the Prophet ﷺ named the command in advance: Zayd ibn Harithah leads; if Zayd falls, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib; if Ja'far falls, Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Abu Qatada's narration keeps what Ja'far said next. He leapt up: 'Messenger of Allah, I fear that you will appoint Zayd over me.' The answer was, 'Carry it out. You do not know what is best of that.'

At Ma'an they learned the size of what was waiting. They had never expected an army like it and spent two nights arguing about whether to send back for instructions. Abdullah ibn Rawahah settled it: the thing you are trying to avoid is exactly the thing you came out looking for.

Zayd took the banner and was killed by a spear thrust. Ja'far took it. He got down, killed his own horse so he could not withdraw, and fought on foot. His right hand was cut off; he held the banner in his left; that was cut off; he clamped it between his upper arms until a Byzantine soldier cut him in two.
layers.hadith_ref: al-Bukhari records that fifty wounds were counted on his body, and not one of them was in his back
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III (narration of Abu Qatada al-Ansari); al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Sahih al-Bukhari and Fath al-Bari

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Two wings, and a household that kept absorbing orphans
layers.content:
After Mu'tah he was called at-Tayyar, the flying one, and Dhu al-Janahayn, the one with two wings — that Allah gave him in exchange two wings to go where he wished in the Garden. The hands he lost holding a piece of cloth upright were traded for that.

When the news of the three commanders reached Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ stood and mentioned them, and Abu Maysara's narration keeps the order and the repetition: 'O Allah, forgive Zayd. O Allah, forgive Zayd. O Allah, forgive Zayd. O Allah, forgive Ja'far and Abdullah ibn Rawahah.'

His house outlived him in an unusual way. Hamzah's orphaned daughter Umama was disputed between Ali, Ja'far and Zayd, each wanting to raise her, and the Prophet ﷺ gave her to Ja'far because his wife Asma bint Umays was the girl's maternal aunt. Twelve martyrs fell at Mu'tah in total; the army came home in order, and within two years the Byzantine frontier was a live question for the whole peninsula.

The lesson in him is not the dying. It is the seven years of speaking carefully in a room full of people paid to trip him up, and then, when there was finally a battle worth having, asking only that he not be put above the freed slave who had been given the flag.
layers.hadith_ref: Narrated by Abu Maysara — the Prophet's supplication for Zayd, Ja'far and Ibn Rawahah, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar

quiz.prompt: What was Ja'far's relationship to Ali ibn Abi Talib?

options.text: His cousin through Abu Talib's brother
His full brother — same father and same mother, Fatima bint Asad
His half-brother through Abu Talib only
His nephew

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — the lineage given at the opening of Ali's entry
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ja'far was the elder. Both were sons of Abu Talib, whose own given name Ibn Sa'd records as Abd Manaf ibn Abd al-Muttalib.

quiz.prompt: Which surah did Ja'far recite when the Negus asked to hear some of the revelation?

options.text: The opening verses of Surah Maryam
Surah al-Fatihah
Surah Yusuf
The end of Surah al-Baqarah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, summarised from Ibn Hisham 1/334-338
quiz.scholar_reflection: He chose the passage on Yahya and Isa. The Negus and his bishops wept, and the king said the two revelations seemed to come from one source.

quiz.prompt: What did Ja'far say when the Prophet ﷺ named the order of command for Mu'tah?

options.text: He asked to be sent home to Makkah instead
He asked that Khalid ibn al-Walid lead
He said he feared being appointed over Zayd
He said nothing at all

quiz.citation: Narrated by Abu Qatada al-Ansari — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'Messenger of Allah, I fear that you will appoint Zayd over me.' The Prophet ﷺ answered, 'Carry it out. You do not know what is best of that.' Ja'far's objection was to outranking Zayd, not to serving under him.

quiz.prompt: How did Ja'far hold the banner after both his hands were severed at Mu'tah?

options.text: He tied it to his saddle
He clasped it between his upper arms
He handed it to Abdullah ibn Rawahah at once
He planted it in the ground and guarded it

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Sahih al-Bukhari
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had already dismounted and killed his own horse so that retreat was not an option. Al-Bukhari records fifty wounds on his body and none of them in his back.

quiz.prompt: According to Ibn Sa'd, how long was Ja'far away from the Prophet ﷺ in Abyssinia?

options.text: About one year
About three years
About seven years
He never left Makkah

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III — Muhammad ibn Umar correcting Ibn Ishaq on the brotherhood pairs
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd uses the fact to correct a chain: Ja'far cannot have been paired in the Madinan brotherhood, because he was in Abyssinia when it happened and 'came seven years later.'

quiz.prompt: Ja'far's great service was done far from the Prophet ﷺ, in a room of strangers. Where does your most useful work actually happen?

options.text: Where I can be seen by the people I answer to
Alone, where nobody is checking
I do better with someone watching, and I know it
It changes entirely depending on the task

quiz.citation: Reflection on the Abyssinia years, The Sealed Nectar and Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Seven years without instructions, without correction, without news. He represented a message he could only hold in memory.

quiz.prompt: He opened his defence by admitting what his people had been. When you have to explain yourself, where do you start?
quiz.slider_label: Honesty about where you came from

options.text: With what I got right
With what I used to be wrong about
With whatever the other person needs to hear
I avoid explaining myself when I can

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ja'far's address to the Negus, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: 'We were an ignorant people.' He was on trial for his life and he began with a confession. That is what made the rest of it credible.

quiz.prompt: He feared being ranked above Zayd, a man who had once been a slave. What does rank do to you?

options.text: I notice it more than I want to admit
I would rather serve than lead
I want the position and I am honest about that
It depends who is being put above me

quiz.citation: Reflection on the narration of Abu Qatada, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ja'far was Banu Hashim, cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, a returning ambassador. His stated fear was of being placed too high.

quiz.prompt: He killed his own horse so that retreat was not available to him. Do you build in escape routes?

options.text: Always — I like knowing I can leave
I commit hard and it sometimes costs me
I say I am committed while keeping an exit quiet
It depends what I am committing to

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, on Ja'far at Mu'tah
quiz.scholar_reflection: It is worth noticing that the army did retreat, in order, under Khalid, and that this was counted as a success. Ja'far's choice was his own, not a rule laid on everyone.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ prayed for Zayd three times before naming Ja'far. What do you make of that order?
quiz.slider_label: Reading the order of a dua

options.text: Zayd needed it most and the Prophet ﷺ knew who needed what
It reflected who fell first, nothing more
It was love — Zayd was the one closest to his heart
I should be careful reading meaning into it at all

quiz.citation: Narrated by Abu Maysara — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Elsewhere in the same volume, when Zayd's daughter wept before him the Prophet ﷺ sobbed, and explained it as the yearning of a lover for the beloved. The narrations sit beside each other without being reconciled.
